items.summary: High-resolution monitoring is fundamental to understand ecosystems dynamics in an era of global change and biodiversity declines. items.title: The interdisciplinary nature of SOIL
items.summary: Abstract. The holistic study of soils requires an interdisciplinary approach involving biologists, chemists, geologists, and physicists, amongst others, something that has been true from the earliest days of the field. The framework species method (FSM) restores forest ecosystems by densely planting open sites, close to natural forest, with woody species, indigenous to the reference ecosystem and selected for their ability to accelerate ecological succession. The method is effective where forest remnants and viable populations of seed dispersers remain. The origins and elements of the FSM are discussed. We review its adoption in 12 countries. items.title: Saplings of significance: Nurturing cultural value of new tree plantings through participatory opportunities
items.summary: Abstract Tree‐planting initiatives are a crucial part of international sustainability and climate action efforts. Yet, many of these initiatives fail to achieve their long‐term sustainability and climate goals. The role of community value is an often‐overlooked factor in promoting the success of new tree plantings. When communities are engaged, the activities offered are often limited to tree planting and maintenance, which can promote social injustices. In this perspective article, we argue that integrating cultural significance considerations into modern tree‐planting initiatives will help to address these issues, centring the voice and values of local communities and taking a long‐term view. We argue that this is key to realising the socio‐environmental goals of new tree plantings and our legacy of us as practitioners. We identify pathways through which cultural significance is generated and suggest activities that could be employed

items.title: What happens after planting? Assessing canopy structure, vegetation cover index, and vegetation distribution of two Miyawaki forest stands in Bengaluru urban district, India
items.summary: Abstract The Miyawaki method, as a technique of forest plantation, is receiving a lot of implementation support and popularity in India and beyond. However, there exists a paucity of scientific data on both pre-implementation baseline and post-implementation monitoring and ecological evaluation of such Miyawaki forest stands (hereafter, MwFS). Quantitative biophysical information on ecological performance is lacking. This study evaluates two MwFS in Bengaluru urban district (India) using canopy measurements and vegetation analysis. Metrics like seasonal vegetation indices and on-ground assessments of canopy closure were done on MwFS with a spectrum of ages indicating canopy closure stabilization at 90-93% in about 60 months. Normalized Green-Red Difference Index calculations on time-series aerial imagery indicate a monotonic progression of seasonal open and closed canopy tree vegetation cover and a general reduction in bare ground cover

items.title: Summary for policymakers of the global assessment report on biodiversity and ecosystem services
items.summary: IPBES is an independent intergovernmental body comprising over 130 member Governments. Established by Governments in 2012, IPBES provides policymakers with objective scientific assessments about the state of knowledge regarding the planet’s biodiversity, ecosystems and the contributions they make to people, as well as options and actions to protect and sustainably use these vital natural assets. The IPBES Global Assessment of Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services represents the landmark product of the first work programme of IPBES (2014-2018). The Global Assessment was initiated following a decision from the IPBES Plenary at its fourth session (IPBES 4, Kuala Lumpur, 2016), and considered by the IPBES Plenary at its seventh session (IPBES 7, Paris, 2019). It is composed of a summary for policymakers, which was approved at IPBES 7, and six chapters, which were accepted at IPBES 7.
